articles.title: Urolithin A Stabilizes CPT1A to Promote HUWE1-Associated NCOA4 Degradation and Alleviate Glucocorticoid-Induced Osteonecrosis of the Femoral Head.
articles.abstract: Glucocorticoid‑induced osteonecrosis of the femoral head (GIONFH) is characterized by impaired osteogenesis, lipid metabolic dysregulation, and trabecular collapse, but its molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study identifies CPT1A‑mediated lipid metabolic homeostasis as a critical protective mechanism against glucocorticoid (GC)‑induced osteogenic injury and ferroptosis. Single‑cell analysis revealed reduced osteoblast abundance and altered lipid metabolism‑related pathways in bone tissue upon GC stimulation. Dexamethasone (DEX) was found to promote lipid deposition, lipid peroxidation, iron overload, mitochondrial impairment, and osteogenic inhibition in both in vitro and in vivo settings; overexpression of CPT1A, however, counteracted these pathological alterations and restored the microarchitecture of the femoral head. Mechanistically, CPT1A directly bound NCOA4 and promoted HUWE1‑mediated K48‑linked ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of NCOA4, thereby limiting NCOA4‑dependent ferritinophagy and ferroptosis. Virtual screening combined with experimental validation identified urolithin A (UA) as a compound that targeted and stabilized CPT1A, enhanced HUWE1‑dependent NCOA4 degradation, suppressed lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis, and restored osteogenic function. Collectively, this study reveals a lipid metabolism-ubiquitination coupling mechanism underlying GIONFH pathogenesis and suggests that targeting CPT1A holds therapeutic potential.

articles.title: IUPHAR Review:PI3Kδ in Cancer: From Biological Functions to Therapeutic Opportunities.
articles.abstract: Phosphoinositide 3-kinase delta (PI3Kδ), encoded by PIK3CD, is a leukocyte-enriched class IA lipid kinase involved in immune receptor signaling, lymphocyte development, and immune homeostasis. Its role in cancer varies across malignancies and cellular compartments, involving tumor-cell-intrinsic signaling, regulation of tumor-associated immune cells, or both. PI3Kδ-directed inhibitors have demonstrated clinical activity in chronic lymphocytic leukemia and indolent B-cell lymphomas; however, serious immune-mediated toxicities and infections have limited the clinical use of several agents. This review examines the molecular mechanisms and therapeutic relevance of PI3Kδ signaling across malignancies, distinguishing direct p110δ-specific evidence from findings involving multiple PI3K isoforms or broader pathway modulation. Selected PI3Kδ-directed inhibitors are evaluated according to their pharmacological profiles, isoform selectivity, dosing strategies, clinical efficacy, safety, and regulatory outcomes. Emerging therapeutic strategies, including biomarker-guided patient selection, rational drug combinations, targeted delivery, and optimized dosing schedules, are discussed in the context of available evidence and limitations. Future progress will depend on identifying disease-specific PI3Kδ dependencies and optimizing target engagement to maintain antitumor activity while minimizing immune toxicity.

articles.title: Modern targeted nerve agent incidents: toxicokinetic complexity, biomarker interpretation and forensic uncertainty.
articles.abstract: Nerve agent poisoning is often linked with mass-casualty events. Typical examples are battlefield use or large terrorist attacks. However, documented incidents from the last decades show a broader and more complex picture. The perspective follows a line of documented cases. It starts with the 1978 ricin "umbrella" murder of Georgi Markov in London (non-nerve agent attack, but historically important). It then moves to the sarin attacks in Matsumoto (1994) and the Tokyo subway (1995), the VX assassinations by the Aum Shinrikyo cult (1994-1995), the 2013 sarin attack in Ghouta and the recent targeted poisonings of Kim Jong-nam (2017), Sergei and Yulia Skripal (2018), Dawn Sturgess and Charlie Rowley (2018) and Alexei Navalny (2020). We use these cases to show how route of exposure, dose, formulation and environmental persistence shape toxicokinetics, clinical presentation, biomarker formation and forensic interpretation. For each case we give the circumstances, the agent, the route, the clinical course, the treatment and the forensic confirmation in detail. We focus on acetylcholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase inhibition, aging, protein adduct formation, dermal absorption and environmental persistence. We describe a recurring "toxicological paradox": greater control over exposure can reduce immediate lethality, but at the same time it increases diagnostic uncertainty and forensic complexity. The cases also show that mass and targeted use are not two separate historical stages. They coexist within the same period, sometimes even within one perpetrator organisation. This perspective has direct implications for emergency preparedness, biomarker development, antidotal treatment windows and international chemical incident response.

articles.title: The conformational-condensate code of GRB2: State switching, spatial organization, and therapeutic windows.
articles.abstract: Growth factor receptor-bound protein 2 (GRB2) is a core adaptor protein that coordinates signals from receptor tyrosine kinases, immune receptors, and metabolic pathways, triggering context-specificcellular responses linked to both normal physiology and disease. While GRB2 has long been defined by its classic interactions-specifically, the binding of its SH2 domain to phosphotyrosine residues and its SH3 domains to proline-rich motifs-emerging research has increasingly revealed it to be a dynamic signaling hub, whose function is governed by conformational switching, inter-domain allostery, and the assembly of biomolecular condensates. Through a combination of structural and biochemical studies, we have come to understand that the equilibria between GRB2 monomers and dimers, domain swapping events, and post-translational modifications work in concert to fine-tune the specificity of its signaling, creating a direct mechanistic link between GRB2 and the development of oncogenesis, immune dysregulation, and insulin resistance. Beyond its well-characterized role in the cytoplasm, GRB2 also localizes to key subcellular compartments including endosomes, lipid rafts, and the nucleus, where it plays a critical role in mediating DNA damage responses. The diversity of GRB2 isoforms, most notably the splice variant Grb3-3, further reshapes cellular signaling networks by modulating the availability of SOS (Son of Sevenless), with far-reaching implications for the pathogenesis of cancer, diabetes, and autoimmune disorders. We propose the "conformational-condensate code" to unify GRB2 regulatory logic: its intrinsic conformational shifts and subcellular condensate assembly jointly determine signaling thresholds under healthy and diseased conditions. From a therapeutic perspective, GRB2 has emerged as a versatile and promising target, with strategies ranging from the inhibition of its SH2 and SH3 domains to allosteric modulation, condensate-directed pharmacology, and the restoration of isoform balance. Notably, antisense oligonucleotides such as prexigebersen (BP1001) have advanced to clinical trials, demonstrating favorable safety profiles and early signs of anti-leukemic activity, while BP1001-A is currently being developed for the treatment of obesity-associated type 2 diabetes-findings that underscore the broad translational potential of targeting GRB2 across a spectrum of diseases.

articles.title: CAR-T in solid tumors: Obstacles and potential strategies.
articles.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapy has achieved remarkable success in treating hematologic malignancies, yet its efficacy in solid tumors remains constrained by multiple challenges. In this review, we summarize the main obstacles hindering CAR-T therapy in solid tumors, including suboptimal antigen targeting, poor trafficking and infiltration into tumor sites, and insufficient persistence of CAR-T cells. Furthermore, we discuss emerging strategies to overcome these hurdles, which can be categorized into two complementary aspects. The first focuses on optimizing intrinsic CAR-T properties for improved adaptation to the tumor microenvironment (TME), such as enriching less-differentiated T cell subsets, modifying CAR constructs, refining ex vivo culture conditions, and modulating specific genes or metabolic pathways through genetic or pharmacological interventions. The second approach aims to remodel the immunosuppressive TME by neutralizing inhibitory mediators, blocking immune checkpoints, and targeting immunosuppressive cell populations and stromal components. Importantly, we also summarized recent progress in in vivo CAR-T therapy. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the obstacles facing CAR-T in solid tumors, addressing both the underlying mechanisms and the translational potential of current and future strategies.

articles.title: Pharmacological agents for promoting diabetic wound healing.
articles.abstract: Diabetic wounds are highly susceptible to chronicity and infection due to impaired healing involving multiple pathophysiological factors. Despite extensive preclinical and clinical research, few approved drugs have been shown to effectively accelerate diabetic wound healing. This review highlights pharmacological interventions for diabetic wound healing, summarizes the current status of drug development, and discusses their potential mechanisms of action. These agents include inflammation-modulating agents, pro-proliferative agents, remodeling-regulating agents, hypoxia- and microcirculation-targeting agents, antioxidant agents, and multi-target agents, such as bioactive constituents from plants and traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) formulas. This review aims to guide future drug development strategies for diabetic wound healing.

articles.title: Coacervate-based materials as emerging vehicles for drug delivery.
articles.abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) is a fundamental mechanism for organizing intracellular biochemical reactions and mediating cellular responses to environmental cues. Inspired by natural membraneless condensates, coacervate-based materials have recently emerged as versatile platforms for drug delivery. Their ability to efficiently encapsulate diverse cargos and release them in response to external or physiological stimuli makes them highly promising for next-generation therapeutic delivery. Despite rapid progress, systematic understanding and design principles for coacervate-based delivery systems remain limited. A comprehensive elucidation of the intermolecular driving forces and mechanisms governing coacervate formation is therefore essential for their rational engineering. This review summarizes the fundamental principles underlying LLPS, fabrication strategies, and characterization techniques of coacervates, followed by recent advances in their applications for delivering small molecules and biomacromolecules. Finally, we discuss current challenges and future opportunities in developing multifunctional, stimuli-responsive coacervates with tunable physicochemical properties. Overall, this review provides insights into the molecular design of coacervate-based systems and highlights their potential in advancing nanomedicine and overcoming biological barriers in drug delivery.

articles.title: Conditionally active antibody‒drug conjugates.
articles.abstract: Conditionally active antibody‒drug conjugates (ADCs) can be achieved through antibody engineering and/or linker-payload design to achieve context-dependent activation, addressing the limitations of conventional ADCs such as premature payload release, inefficient tumor penetration, and on-target, off-tumor toxicities. Antibody surfaces can be modified with steric shields, site-specific conjugation, or reversible masking groups to further limit off-target binding. Linker-payloads are masked in circulation through prodrug strategies, such as multi-step or logic-gated linkers, releasable caps, or bioorthogonal chemistries. These strategies confine cytotoxic drugs to the tumor microenvironment (TME), enhancing intratumoral drug concentration, expanding the therapeutic window, and reducing systemic toxicity. Early clinical studies of conditionally active ADCs targeting ROR2, AXL, and CD71 have demonstrated promising safety and efficacy. This review discusses the underlying mechanisms, antibody engineering and linker-payload design strategies, and clinical progress of conditionally active ADCs, and considers future avenues to improve tumor selectivity and therapeutic performance.

articles.title: Molecular smugglers in obesity-driven MASLD: Snitching on adipose-derived extracellular vesicles.
articles.abstract: Obesity-related adipose tissue (AT) dysfunction is closely associated with the development and progression of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), the most prevalent chronic liver disease. Emerging evidence highlights that the AT-liver crosstalk is mediated by AT-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) that exacerbate the progression of MASLD during obesity. During obesity development, AT undergoes pathological remodeling characterized by hypertrophic adipocytes, pro-inflammatory macrophages, dysfunctional adipose-derived stem cells (ADSCs), and increased cellular heterogeneity, which collectively alter the composition and function of secreted EVs. AT-derived EVs enter the circulation and transport bioactive cargo, including microRNAs (miRNAs), mtDNA, proteins and lipids to the liver, where they can modulate hepatocellular metabolism, liver inflammation and fibrogenesis. This review outlines the current state of knowledge on AT-derived EVs during MASLD, emphasizing the dynamic changes in AT under metabolic stress as well as the interactions between AT-derived EVs and the liver. We further explore the potential of EVs and their associated molecules as noninvasive biomarkers and potential therapeutic targets and underscore that understanding AT-liver communication via EVs offers perspectives for precision medicine in MASLD.

articles.title: Spatiotemporal crosstalk of post-translational modifications: A therapeutic avenue in spinal cord injury.
articles.abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) triggers irreversible neurological dysfunction driven by sequential primary and secondary insults, with neuronal death and neuroinflammation as the central pathological determinants. Despite advances in neuroregeneration research, an incomplete understanding of the molecular regulators underlying these processes limits the development of effective SCI treatment strategies. Post-translational modifications (PTMs) function as critical "dynamic molecular switches" that spatiotemporally regulate protein function and signaling cascades, shaping the SCI microenvironment. Emerging evidence suggests that interdependent PTM networks-rather than isolated modifications-regulate the balance between deterioration and repair. This review synthesizes current insights into seven major PTMs implicated in neuronal death and neuroinflammation after SCI, emphasizing their cooperative crosstalk and the methodological challenges in decoding their temporal dynamics. We propose a "spatiotemporally regulated PTM network" framework to guide therapeutic interventions, highlighting multiplex PTM modulation as a promising strategy to enhance neuronal survival, reduce neuroinflammation, and promote functional recovery after SCI. This review deepens the understanding of PTM crosstalk in SCI pathology and provides new perspectives for developing novel PTM detection and clinical therapeutic strategies.

articles.title: In vivo CAR-T therapy: Delivery systems and beyond for addressing expression, persistence, and safety challenges.
articles.abstract: The clinical translation of ex vivo CAR-T therapy is constrained by its complex manufacturing processes, limited treatment accessibility, and the toxicities associated with lymphodepleting chemotherapy. In vivo CAR-T strategies, which utilize viral or non-viral vectors to reprogram a patient's T cells directly in situ genetically, offer a promising alternative. This review provides a systematic examination of the critical barriers impeding the advancement of in vivo CAR-T therapy. We first summarize the factors influencing the targeting ability of both the delivery system and the CAR molecule. As for the vectors, we detail how the composition and physicochemical properties of LNPs shift their tropism from the liver to the spleen and provide a critical comparison of active targeting strategies based on different T-cell surface antigens. As for the CAR molecule, target selection is primarily dictated by the intended disease. Furthermore, we discuss the determinants of poor CAR-T cell persistence, including unstable mRNA payloads and exhaustion-associated signaling pathways. Addressing the challenges of solid tumor treatment, we dissect the multifaceted role of the tumor microenvironment. Finally, this review illustrates the mechanisms underlying overactivation and immunogenicity triggered by both viral and non-viral vector systems.

articles.title: Safety and Tolerability of Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter-2 Inhibitors: A State-of-the-Art Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT-2is) have evolved from glucose-lowering agents to foundational therapies for the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease, with substantial benefits for cardiovascular, kidney, and survival outcomes. As their indications continue to expand, a comprehensive understanding of their safety and tolerability has become increasingly important for optimizing patient care. Building on our recent state-of-the-art review of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, this review provides a contemporary synthesis of the evidence on the safety and tolerability of SGLT-2is. We critically appraise data from randomized controlled trials, cardiovascular and kidney outcome trials, pharmacovigilance databases, large observational studies, and systematic reviews and meta-analyses. The available evidence demonstrates that SGLT-2is have a favorable overall safety profile, with genital mycotic infections representing the most consistently observed adverse event. Volume depletion and euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis remain clinically important but are uncommon and are largely preventable through appropriate patient selection, patient education, and temporary treatment interruption during high-risk clinical situations. Fournier's gangrene should be regarded as a very rare but serious complication requiring prompt recognition and treatment. In contrast, randomized trials and meta-analyses generally indicate a reduced risk of acute kidney injury, while evidence concerning fracture, lower-limb amputation, hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, and cancer is less definitive. Although consistent class-wide increases in these latter outcomes have not been established, uncommon or agent-specific risks cannot be excluded, particularly where event numbers are small or follow-up is limited. Overall, treatment discontinuation because of adverse events is low across major cardiovascular, heart failure, and kidney outcome trials, supporting the excellent tolerability of this therapeutic class. Comparative evidence suggests only modest differences among individual SGLT-2is, although definitive conclusions remain limited by the absence of direct, large, randomized head-to-head trials. We also summarize practical strategies for adverse-event mitigation, monitoring, temporary treatment interruption, and individualized patient selection. As the clinical applications of SGLT-2is continue to broaden, ongoing pharmacovigilance, inclusive clinical trials, and comparative safety studies will be essential to further refine their benefit-risk profile and optimize their safe use across diverse patient populations.

articles.title: Targeting P23 by PM534 suppresses glioblastoma via disruption of SFPQ-mediated phase separation.
articles.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is one of the most lethal human malignancies, with a five-year survival rate of approximately 5% and limited effective therapeutic options beyond standard-of-care regimens, underscoring an urgent need for novel therapeutic agents and druggable targets. Here, we report that PM534, a marine sponge-derived synthetic compound, potently suppresses GBM malignancy in orthotopic patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models and in vitro, with IC50 value of 1.86nM in patient-derived GBM#P3 cells. Target identification via activity-based protein profiling (ABPP) revealed P23, a co-chaperone of HSP90, as the direct molecular target of PM534. Subsequent LC-MS/MS analysis, molecular dynamics simulation, and site-directed mutagenesis collectively demonstrated that PM534 covalently bond P23 at Cys58 and Cys75. P23 demonstrated significant upregulation in human GBM tissues and orthotopic PDX models, correlating with tumor progression. Mechanistic studies exhibited that P23 interacted with splicing factor proline- and glutamine-rich protein (SFPQ) to regulate liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). Covalent engagement of P23 by PM534 disrupted the interaction of SFPQ with the HSP90/P23 complex, thereby triggering proteasomal degradation of SFPQ and consequently abrogating SFPQ-driven LLPS and oncogenic condensate formation. These findings establish PM534 as a promising drug candidate for clinical GBM therapy and highlight P23 as a therapeutic target in GBM.

articles.title: Macrophage-targeted GAS6 siRNA delivery by a multifunctional mannan-peptide nanocarrier attenuates pulmonary fibrosis progression.
articles.abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a fatal interstitial lung disease with limited treatment options. Here, we investigated MR3, a macrophage-targeted polysaccharide-peptide delivery system, for the pulmonary delivery of siRNA against growth arrest-specific protein 6 (GAS6). MR3 facilitated effective siRNA endosomal escape, while intratracheal administration ensured sustained lung retention with targeted uptake by macrophages. Functionally, siGAS6@MR3 selectively downregulated macrophage GAS6 expression to inhibit profibrotic M2 polarization, thereby improving survival, restoring lung function, and reversing histological and molecular indices of fibrosis in IPF models. Furthermore, MR3 conferred intrinsic antioxidant protection that enhanced macrophage survival under oxidative stress. siGAS6@MR3 was well tolerated in long-term repeat-dose studies, with no evidence of systemic toxicity. These findings identify GAS6 as a promising antifibrotic target and establish MR3 as a versatile, macrophage-selective siRNA platform for fibrotic and other macrophage-driven diseases.

articles.title: Enzyme-driven Janus nanomotor for enhanced diabetic wound healing via deep penetration-mediated biofilm eradication and hypoxia alleviation.
articles.abstract: Diabetic chronic wounds represent an urgent clinical challenge due to persistent biofilm infections, tissue hypoxia, and impaired healing, leading to prolonged morbidity and high healthcare burden. Herein, we develop a self-propelled Janus nanomotor (GCO@AM) to overcome the biofilm barrier and modulate the diabetic wound microenvironment. The nanomotor consists of an Au/Pt-coated spherical head functionalized with an S. aureus-targeting peptide and an enzyme-loaded mesoporous silica rod tail. Under the acidic and hyperglycemic biofilm microenvironment, a cascade reaction involving glucose oxidase (GOx), catalase (CAT), and calcium peroxide (CaO2) generates oxygen gas (O2) in situ, producing asymmetric propulsion that drives directional motion toward S. aureus. The generated O2 alleviates local hypoxia, while the Au/Pt head catalyzes O2 into bactericidal superoxide radicals (O2•-) for bacterial elimination. GCO@AM exhibits enhanced biofilm penetration, achieving a 15.2-fold increase in penetration depth compared with non-motile nanoparticles, and eradicates 99.98% of bacteria within S. aureus biofilms in vitro. In diabetic wound models, GCO@AM effectively removes biofilm infections, relieves hypoxia, reduces inflammation, promotes angiogenesis and collagen deposition, and achieves a wound closure rate of 98.20% within 10 days. This work establishes a biofilm-responsive self-propelled nanomotor that integrates targeted delivery, antibacterial therapy, and microenvironment modulation for treating chronic biofilm-associated wounds.

articles.title: Calibrating public genome archives for AMR surveillance: Four decades of redundancy-aware phylogenomics of pandemic Escherichia coli ST131.
articles.abstract: AIMS: Escherichia coli sequence type (ST)131 is a globally disseminated multidrug-resistant pathogen, yet public genome collections are skewed by uneven sampling and repeated sequencing of genetically near-identical isolates. Rather than another reconstruction of ST131 evolution, we quantified redundancy, reassessed population structure, and tested how sampling bias affects estimates of phylogenetic diversity, clade-specific dating, and fluoroquinolone-resistance-associated diversification. METHODS: EnteroBase core-genome multilocus sequence typing (cgMLST) hierarchical clustering was used to reduce redundancy among 16,713 public ST131 complex genomes. Representative public genomes were combined with 390 unpublished New Zealand ST131 surveillance genomes from 1999 to 2019. Clade-specific phylogenetic and temporal analyses were performed for Clades A, B, and C, with sensitivity analyses using stricter cgMLST clustering and phylogenetic-diversity-guided subsampling. RESULTS: Public genomes were highly redundant: just 2/409 cgMLST groups contained 85.2% of public genomes. After redundancy reduction, dated Clades A, B, and C phylogenies spanning 1999-2023 (n = 113), 1982-2025 (n = 240), and 1999-2025 (n = 614), respectively, were constructed. Clades A and B showed distinct temporal histories and evolutionary rates. Date-randomization supported temporal information in Clade C, although incomplete convergence of the observed-date relaxed-clock and Bayesian Skyline analyses means that exact Clade C molecular-date and demographic estimates should be interpreted cautiously. The broad Clade C reconstruction nevertheless indicated expansion of the dominant fluoroquinolone-resistant lineage in the late 1990s/early 2000s and again in the mid-2000s. CONCLUSIONS: Public ST131 datasets reflect sampling distribution as well as number of available genomes. Redundancy in dominant cgMLST groups can obscure uncommon lineages and blur emergence with later expansion. In Clade C, redundancy-aware analysis was broadly consistent with previous estimates placing major fluoroquinolone-resistant diversification in the early 1990s, while indicating that early resistance diversification preceded later amplification of resistant sublineages.

articles.title: Isoliquiritigenin attenuates doxorubicin-induced cardiomyopathy by alleviating mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative damage through the Piezo1/Ca²⁺/Pdk4 signaling axis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Doxorubicin (DOX) is widely employed as an antineoplastic agent in clinical settings, yet its therapeutic utility is constrained by dose-dependent cardiotoxicity, partly resulting from oxidative injury to cardiomyocytes and impairment of mitochondrial function. Hence, there is an urgent imperative to develop cardioprotective strategies targeting oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. Previous studies have suggested that isoliquiritigenin (Iso) confers protection against DOX-induced cardiomyopathy (DIC); however, the exact molecular mechanisms governing its pharmacological activity have yet to be elucidated. PURPOSE: The objective of this study was to further explore the cardioprotective effects conferred by isoliquiritigenin (Iso) and to clarify the potential molecular mechanisms involved. METHODS /STUDY DESIGNS: Oxidative stress, mitochondrial function, myocardial injury, and intracellular calcium levels were examined in cardiomyocytes. In addition, mechanistic investigations were conducted using cardiomyocyte-specific Piezo1-knockdown mice generated by AAV9, along with EGTA treatment for calcium depletion, Piezo1 knockdown, and Pdk4 overexpression in cardiomyocytes. RESULTS: Treatment with Iso was found to significantly attenuate DOX-induced myocardial injury, histopathological damage, and apoptosis of cardiomyocytes in vivo. Moreover, in vitro experiments corroborated that Iso effectively rescued H9c2 cells and NMCMs from DOX-induced cytotoxicity, oxidative stress, and apoptosis. Further investigations revealed that isoliquiritigenin (Iso) preserved mitochondrial function through suppression of oxidative stress damage and restoration of the equilibrium between mitochondrial fusion and fission. The underlying mechanism revealed that Iso exerts its effects by targeting the Piezo1 mechanosensitive channel and subsequently modulating Pdk4 via Ca²⁺ signaling. CONCLUSION: Collectively, our findings suggest that the cardioprotective efficacy of Iso against DOX-induced cardiotoxicity is mediated by the Piezo1-Ca²⁺-Pdk4 signaling pathway, which operates to attenuate oxidative insults, preserve mitochondrial integrity, and reduce apoptotic loss of cardiac myocytes.

articles.title: Inhalation of Gardenia jasminoides flower essential oil attenuates stress-associated neurobehavioral abnormalities in mice.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Gardenia jasminoides Ellis is a traditional medicinal and aromatic plant, but the neurobehavioral potential of its flower-derived essential oil remains insufficiently understood. PURPOSE: This study aimed to evaluate whether G. jasminoides flower essential oil (GEO) inhalation attenuates chronic stress-associated neurobehavioral abnormalities and to characterize the accompanying hippocampal, metabolic, and gut microbial responses. METHODS: GEO was chemically profiled by headspace solid-phase microextraction coupled with gas chromatography-mass spectrometry and evaluated in a chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) mouse model. Mice were exposed to GEO by inhalation during the final 2 weeks of the 6-week CUMS procedure. Behavioral performance was assessed using the open field test, elevated plus maze, tail suspension test, forced swim test, and sucrose preference test. Hippocampal morphology, inflammatory and oxidative stress-related indices, neurochemical markers, serum corticosterone, serum metabolomics, hippocampal transcriptomics, gut microbiota composition, and hippocampal neuroimmune/synaptic signaling markers were further analyzed. RESULTS: Chemical profiling tentatively annotated 59 volatile constituents in GEO, with linalool and linalyl acetate identified as the predominant constituents. GEO inhalation attenuated CUMS-associated behavioral abnormalities, with significant changes observed most consistently in the GEO-20 group. GEO exposure was also associated with increased hippocampal dendritic spine density relative to the CUMS group, lower inflammatory and oxidative stress-related indices, higher hippocampal brain-derived neurotrophic factor, γ-aminobutyric acid, and 5-hydroxytryptamine levels, and lower serum corticosterone. Serum metabolomics identified GEO-20-associated changes in metabolic features and pathways involving nucleotide/purine metabolism, arachidonic acid-related lipid mediator pathways, bile acid-related metabolism, and neuroactive metabolic processes. Hippocampal transcriptomics identified GEO-20-associated changes in neuroimmune-, neuroactive ligand-receptor-, and γ-aminobutyric acid synapse-related transcriptional profiles. Gut microbiota analysis revealed GEO-20-associated changes in microbial richness, community composition, discriminatory taxa, and genus-level co-occurrence patterns. Targeted molecular assays showed lower hippocampal glial reactivity and inflammatory signaling-related markers after GEO exposure, whereas GEO-20 was associated with higher levels of mitochondrial regulatory and synaptic plasticity markers. CONCLUSION: GEO inhalation attenuated chronic stress-associated neurobehavioral abnormalities in mice and was accompanied by changes in hippocampal neuroimmune and synaptic plasticity-related markers, together with broader systemic metabolic and microbial responses.

articles.title: Omega-3 PUFAs in the prevention of radiation-induced esophagitis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIM: Omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) have anti-inflammatory and tissue-protective properties. This study aimed to investigate the role and potential mechanism of PUFAs in preventing acute radiation esophagitis (ARE). METHODS: A murine ARE model was established, and multi-omics analyzes, including proteomics, metabolomics, and single-cell RNA sequencing, were performed as well as in vitro experiments using human esophageal epithelial cells. A retrospective clinical analysis was performed to evaluate the effects of deep-sea fish oil (FO) containing omega-3 PUFAs. RESULTS: In the mouse ARE model, esophagus proteomic analysis revealed that, compared with irradiation (IR), IR + docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) resulted in greater enrichment of proteins in the mitochondrial inner membrane and oxidative phosphorylation pathways. Furthermore, metabolomics revealed significantly reduced levels of radiation-induced metabolic products such as Cer 17:1;2O/16:0;(2OH), Cer 18:0;3O/16:0, LPC 40:7, lactobionic acid, and pantetheine after IR, and the addition of DHA significantly reversed these changes. In human esophageal epithelial cells (HEECs), omega-3 PUFAs mitigated irradiation-induced mitochondrial damage by modulating respiratory chain proteins, reducing intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels and enhancing cell viability. Single-cell RNA sequencing showed that DHA addition reshaped intercellular communication and inflammatory signaling, and also modulated the cell fate trajectories of fibroblasts and endothelial cells in irradiated mouse esophageal tissues. Our retrospective investigation found that FO supplementation significantly reduced ARE severity (odds ratio=0.36, p=0.006) and pain scores (p=0.018) in esophageal cancer patients undergoing radiotherapy compared with those in patients receiving radiotherapy alone. CONCLUSION: Omega-3 PUFAs can prevent ARE mainly by regulating mitochondrial metabolism, intercellular communication networks, inflammatory signaling, and the fate trajectories of fibroblasts and endothelial cells. The potential anti-ARE effect of FO requires more clinical trials for verification.

articles.title: Concurrent low-dose-rate gamma irradiation and inorganic arsenite: genotoxicity and transcriptional responses in liver and testis in CBA and C57BL/6 mice.
articles.abstract: Humans in arsenic-endemic and radiologically exposed settings may be co-exposed to inorganic arsenic and ionizing radiation, yet the combined effects of chronic low-dose-rate irradiation and environmentally relevant arsenic are poorly defined. In a single factorial experiment, male CBA and C57BL/6N mice were exposed to sodium arsenite in drinking water (0, 0.3 or 3 mg/L) and chronic γ irradiation (2.5 mGy/h, total 3 Gy), alone and combined. We measured blood genotoxicity (comet and micronucleus assays), characterised 21 circulating miRNAs, global DNA methylation and sequenced liver and testis transcriptomes to identify significant pathways. Arsenite exposure was accompanied by an increase in FPG-sensitive DNA lesions in white blood cells alongside a slight reduction in single strand breaks. Micronucleus frequency in reticulocytes and erythrocytes was not affected by arsenite. Arsenite was identified as an oxidative rather than a chromosomal genotoxicant. Only one miRNA (miR-133a-5p) responded clearly to arsenite. Global DNA methylation was only affected by irradiation. The liver and testis transcriptomes shared common DNA-repair and oxidative-stress pathways, but the organs diverged in response. Irradiation was the dominant stressor while the effect of the concurrent arsenite exposure was additive, antagonistic or synergistic. Baseline strain differences were large but additive, with negligible strain × treatment interaction in the transcriptome, whereas strain × arsenite interactions were found for the FPG-comet signal and hepatic arsenic. Our study contributes new data, experimental design and analysis methods about the genotoxic and transcriptional landscape of multiple stressor exposure.

articles.title: Stress granule assembly drives an adaptive survival response in keratinocytes under TiO2 nanoparticles and UV irradiation.
articles.abstract: Nanoscale processing enhances the photocatalytic reactivity of titanium dioxide nanoparticles (TiO2 NPs) under UV exposure. While these nanoparticles are widely utilized in cosmetics and industrial formulations, the molecular decision-making processes that dictate keratinocyte survival following UV exposure remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that concurrent exposure to TiO2 NPs and UVA radiation induces substantial synergistic phototoxicity, which does not occur under individual exposure at the same respective doses. Under phototoxic conditions, keratinocytes were found to engage an adaptive response characterized by G3BP1-dependent stress granule (SG) assembly to mitigate cellular stress. Mechanistically, this cytoprotective response was driven by PERK/eIF2α signaling and coordinated by endoplasmic reticulum-mediated calcium flux. Pharmacological inhibition of SG assembly or genetic knockdown of G3BP1 exacerbated cell death, indicating that SG formation serves as a cytoprotective mechanism that relieves proteotoxic burden. Collectively, these findings delineate a proteostatic defense mechanism against TiO2-mediated phototoxicity, providing fundamental insights for the safe-by-design evaluation of advanced dermatological materials.

articles.title: Navigating the Role of Clinical Pharmacists in Integrative Oncology Care Teams: Time to Create Higher Training and Practice Standards.
articles.abstract: Integrative oncology (IO) programs are committed to offer evidence-based complementary medicine within conventional cancer care, addressing quality of life-related concerns. As part of a multidisciplinary team, clinical pharmacists provide guidance on potential effectiveness and safety of herbal supplement use, identifying potential toxicities and herb-drug interactions. In this commentary, we discuss the need to establish clinical competencies based on a structured training syllabus addressing patients' preferences and expectations, while ensuring safe IO practices.

articles.title: Portulaca oleracea L.-derived extracellular vesicle-like particles reprogram intestinal ILCs to alleviate inflammatory bowel disease and colitis-associated colorectal cancer.
articles.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and its progression to colitis-associated colorectal cancer (CAC) pose significant clinical challenges due to their complex pathogenesis and limited therapeutic options. Plant-derived extracellular vesicle-like particles (PEVLPs) have emerged as promising candidates for targeted therapy, owing to their biocompatibility and intrinsic bioactivity. Here, we isolated and characterized Portulaca oleracea L.-derived extracellular vesicle-like particles (PO-EVLPs) and demonstrated their preferential accumulation in the colon of mouse models through systematic biodistribution studies. Mechanistically, PO-EVLPs exert therapeutic effects via the delivery of miRNAs. Specifically, the enriched miR159-y suppresses TGF-β receptor expression, thereby promoting the expansion of group three innate lymphoid cells (ILC3s) in colitic tissues. Furthermore, during the transition from chronic inflammation to carcinogenesis, miR159-y-mediated inhibition of TGF-β receptors prevents TGF-β-driven differentiation of NK cells into ILC1s and the conversion of ILC3s into regulatory innate lymphoid cells (ILCregs), thereby impeding CAC progression. In vivo studies also indicated a favorable safety profile. These findings establish PEVLPs as a multifunctional therapeutic platform that simultaneously targets inflammatory pathways and neoplastic transformation, offering a novel strategy for managing IBD and CAC by precisely modulating mucosal immunity.

articles.title: Precise unidirection delivery and site-specific release utilizing a nanocapsules-loaded mucoadhesive in situ gel: Targeted eradication of Helicobacter pylori and gastric homeostasis restoration.
articles.abstract: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection disrupts the gastric microenvironment and promotes the development of gastric cancer and other gastrointestinal diseases. Despite the high prevalence of asymptomatic chronic infection and recurrent infections, persistent mucosal injury continues to drive early pathological alterations, including gastric epithelial remodeling and intestinal metaplasia, that may become irreversible beyond a "point of no return". Although clinical antibiotic-based H. pylori eradication therapies reduce gastric cancer risk, their efficacy markedly diminishes once progressive gastric premalignant lesions developed, and long-term use often causes microbiome dysbiosis and antimicrobial resistance. To address these unmet clinical needs, we developed CurE-gel, an antibiotic-free smart in situ gel with pH- and lipase-cascade responsive drug release. This system enables targeted eradication of H. pylori while simultaneously facilitating gastric niche restoration. Composed of sodium alginate and polyacrylate, CurE-gel exhibits strong gastric mucosal adhesion and precise pH responsiveness. Utilizing the pathophysiological gastric pH gradient (luminal pH 1-2 vs. mucosal pH > 4), CurE-gel mediates unidirectional release of its encapsulated nanocapsules (CurE-cap) at the damaged mucosal side. Then, CurE-cap penetrates the mucus and accumulated at H. pylori colonies, where its polycaprolactone shell is hydrolyzed by bacterial lipase to release curcumin and eugenol. This system achieved: (i) targeted H. pylori eradication via biofilm disruption and virulence suppression; (ii) epithelial barrier protection and pathological progression suppression through virulence translocation inhibition, ROS scavenging, lipid peroxidation reduction and DNA damage mitigation; and (iii) gastric homeostasis restoration by recovery of tight junction proteins and gastric microbiota modulation. In vivo, CurE-gel achieved over 99% H. pylori eradication, reversed gastric progressive premalignant lesions and reconstructed a healthy gastric microbiota without systemic toxicity. By integrating mucoadhesive retention with pH- and lipase-cascade responsive drug release, this platform sets an innovative paradigm for two-pronged strategy in targeted H. pylori clearance and gastric homeostasis restoration, ultimately aiming to prevent gastric carcinogenesis.

articles.title: In situ hydrogel nanovaccine based on whole-cell tumor antigen efficiently activates adaptive immunity for the prevention and treatment of ovarian cancer.
articles.abstract: Due to the late diagnosis with widespread peritoneal metastases and frequent chemoresistance, ovarian cancer has limited survival rates and necessitates innovative therapies. Here, we present an in situ hydrogel nanovaccine (LCMP@ALG) for spatiotemporally-synchronized antigen-adjuvant delivery to stimulate robust antitumor immunity. The hydrogel continuously releases mannosylated nanoparticles LCMP which are effectively internalized by dendritic cells and actively accumulate in lymph nodes via the ligand-mediated targeting effect. Benefiting from autologous tumor cell lysates, the vaccines evade antigen-specific tolerance. LCMP can synergistically activate Toll-like receptor 4 and Toll-like receptor 9 to augment antigen processing and cross-presentation, further potentiating the activation of humoral and cellular antitumor immunity. In the mouse model, the vaccine LCMP@ALG induces specific antitumor responses as well as long-term immunological memory. When combined with Programmed cell death protein 1 blockade, LCMP@ALG demonstrates a superior efficacy in prevention and elimination of ovarian cancer.

articles.title: Glutaminolysis inhibition boosts cuproptosis to eliminate breast cancer stem cells.
articles.abstract: The metabolic plasticity of cancer stem cells (CSCs) enables them to adaptively switch between glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation, and alternative fuels such as glutamine and fatty acids, promoting tumorigenesis and progression by ensuring survival under diverse environmental stresses. However, current therapeutic approaches targeting CSCs remain limited, particularly those relying on single metabolic interventions. By leveraging concurrent metabolic modulation and redox disruption to sensitize CSCs to cuproptosis, we prepared a polydopamine/hydroxyethyl starch-based nanoplatform (CH@PHF) for co-delivering copper-diethyldithiocarbamate (CuET) and HYL001. Specifically, HYL001 suppresses glutaminase (GLS) activity, thereby blocking glutamine metabolism and inhibiting glutathione (GSH) biosynthesis. This effect synergizes with CuET to collectively amplify oxidative stress in CSCs. Furthermore, the combination of HYL001 and CuET significantly elevates intracellular copper levels, particularly the cuprous form (Cu+), thereby sensitizing CSCs to cuproptosis. This combined treatment effectively inhibits tumor growth and metastasis by targeting and eradicating breast cancer stem cells (BCSCs), offering a promising avenue for tumor therapy.

articles.title: Identification of flupirtine as a candidate against liver fibrosis in mice: Preserving mitochondria quality by suppressing calpain 1/complex I/mtROS axis via targeting asparagine synthase.
articles.abstract: Liver fibrosis is a pressing clinical challenge, poses a huge threat to human health. However, there is no approved therapeutic medication to treat this devastating disease. Using a drug repositioning or drug rescue (DDDR) strategy, we identified the anti-analgesic agent flupirtine as a potential anti-liver fibrosis candidate through cell-based high-throughput screening of the FDA-approved drug library. Treatment with flupirtine reversed TGF-β1-induced fibrogenesis and ameliorated liver fibrosis in CCl4 or DDC diet-treated fibrotic mice. Asparagine synthase (ASNS) was identified as the direct target of flupirtine. Flupirtine interacted with the residues Asp 401 and Arg 404 of ASNS, thereby inhibiting its enzymatic activity. Importantly, ASNS levels were increased in activated hepatic stellate cells (acHSCs) and in the livers of fibrotic mice and humans, and are positively correlated with the severity of liver fibrosis. Mechanistically, inhibition or deletion of ASNS to increase l-aspartate levels reversed TGF-β1-induced Ca2+ overload in mitochondria, leading to suppression of calpain 1/complex I/mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) axis, thereby improving mitochondrial quality and enhancing mitochondrial oxidation, ultimately counteracting liver fibrosis. Our study identified ASNS as a potential therapeutic target for treating liver fibrosis, flupirtine counteracted liver fibrosis in mice by suppressing ASNS in acHSCs, thereby blocking mitochondrial Ca2+/calpain 1/complex I/mtROS axis.

articles.title: Targeting the USP13-ACLY axis in tumor endothelial cells: Ginsenoside Rd suppresses pathological angiogenesis through metabolic-epigenetic reprogramming.
articles.abstract: ATP citrate lyase (ACLY) is a pivotal enzyme implicated in cancer cells' aberrant survival and proliferation. However, its precise role in tumor endothelial cells (TECs) in tumor angiogenesis and malignant progression remains poorly defined. Our previous studies have identified a high distribution of ginsenoside Rd in TECs, yet the mechanism underlying its anti-angiogenic properties has not been elucidated. Here, we clarify the direct regulatory effects of ACLY in TECs and explain how Rd reprograms the ACLY metabolic pathway in TECs. Systemic Acly silencing in tumor models resulted in suppressed angiogenesis and tumor progression. Importantly, TEC-specific Acly knockdown directly disrupted pathological vascularization and exerted comparable inhibitory effects on tumor growth. Metabolomic profiling revealed that ginsenoside Rd reduced nuclear acetyl-coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA) levels by down-regulating ACLY expression, thereby inhibiting the transcription of angiogenesis-related factors through reduced acetylation of histone H3 (but not H4). Mechanistically, ginsenoside Rd promotes the ubiquitin-mediated degradation of ACLY by targeting and suppressing ubiquitin-specific peptidase 13 (USP13). This study not only establishes a mechanistic framework for the development of ACLY-centric therapeutic strategies to reprogram pathological vasculature but also identifies the natural compound Rd as a pharmacological modulator of TECs metabolism via targeting the USP13-ACLY axis.

articles.title: Aspirin induces glycolytic reprogramming via lysine salicylation of ALDOA.
articles.abstract: Aspirin (ASA), a classical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug, is known to inhibit glycolysis in cancer cells; however, the underlying mechanism remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify lysine salicylation (Ksa) as an ASA-dependent protein modification that suppresses glycolysis and proliferation in colorectal cancer cells. Specifically, ASA causes Ksa on the key glycolytic enzyme aldolase A (ALDOA), markedly reducing its enzymatic activity without altering protein level. Metabolomic analysis revealed that ASA impairs the conversion of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (F16BP) to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (GAP), thereby disrupting glycolytic flux. In a xenograft mouse model, ASA administration not only inhibited tumor growth but also enhanced ALDOA Ksa level and blocked F16BP-to-GAP conversion. Besides, site-directed mutagenesis and genetic code expansion experiments confirmed that ALDOA K13sa is critical for ASA-mediated inhibition of glycolysis and cancer cell proliferation. Together, this study uncovers Ksa as an innovative mechanism by which ASA affects glycolysis and cancer cell proliferation, providing further insights into its potential role in cancer prevention and therapy.

articles.title: TP53 mutation promotes sunitinib resistance in gallbladder cancer via the ARHGEF7-AS2/miR-326/AXL pathway.
articles.abstract: Gallbladder cancer (GBC) is an aggressive digestive malignancy with poor prognosis and frequent treatment resistance. Aberrant receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling is common in GBC and supports use of RTK inhibitors (RTKis) such as sunitinib, yet clinical responses remain limited and the mechanisms driving resistance are unclear. In this study, we utilized patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models of GBC and conducted RNA microarray profiling alongside whole-exome sequencing to identify differentially expressed long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) and gene mutations associated with sunitinib resistance. Our findings reveal a novel resistance mechanism whereby TP53 loss impairs its binding to the transcription factor SP1, resulting in SP1-mediated transcriptional activation of the lncRNA ARHGEF7-AS2. Upregulation of ARHGEF7-AS2 functions as a competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) that sequesters miR-326, thereby relieving repression of its target gene AXL and activating the downstream AKT signaling cascade. This regulatory axis promotes resistance to sunitinib in GBC cells. Importantly, inhibition of ARHGEF7-AS2 or pharmacological blockade of the AXL/AKT pathway restored sunitinib sensitivity, underscoring the therapeutic potential of targeting this pathway. Collectively, our study identifies a previously unrecognized TP53/ARHGEF7-AS2/miR-326/AXL signaling axis that contributes to sunitinib resistance in GBC, providing new mechanistic insights and potential avenues for therapeutic intervention in advanced disease.

articles.title: Discovery and preclinical evaluation of ZLC853 as a potential clinical candidate covalently targeting CDK12/13 kinases.
articles.abstract: Previous studies highlight the therapeutic promise of inhibiting cyclin-dependent kinases 12 and 13 (CDK12/13) for castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) and other malignancies. However, developing small molecule modulators of CDK12/13 that exhibit an optimal combination of potency, selectivity and favorable pharmacokinetics (PK) remains challenging. In this study, we present ZLC853, a potent, selective, and orally bioavailable covalent inhibitor of CDK12/13 developed through PK-oriented optimization of our previously reported inhibitor YJZ5118. ZLC853 potently inhibited CDK12 and CDK13 with IC50 values of 40.0 and 18.2 nmol/L, respectively, and displayed exceptional kinase selectivity in a comprehensive KinomeScan assay. Its covalent binding mechanism was unequivocally validated through mass spectrometry, co-crystal structure analysis, cellular pull-down assays, and washout experiments. Functionally, ZLC853 suppressed the transcription of DNA damage response genes, induced DNA damage, and promoted apoptosis. Additionally, ZLC853 exhibited good oral bioavailability and robust antitumor activity across multiple prostate cancer models, both in vitro and in vivo, supporting it as a promising candidate for clinical investigation.

articles.title: Mendelian randomization-inspired targeted polyphenol nanoplatform for synergistic osteoarthritis therapy.
articles.abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a debilitating joint disorder with few disease-modifying treatments. Inspired by a Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis of over 470,000 individuals that identified a causal association between green tea consumption and a reduced risk of OA, this study developed a multifunctional nanomedicine (Dex@TPNs-FA, denoted as DTF) by encapsulating dexamethasone (Dex) in self-assembled tea polyphenol nanoparticles (TPNs) modified with folic acid for targeted delivery to synovial macrophages. DTF reduced inflammation and oxidative stress, inhibited apoptosis, and promoted cartilage matrix synthesis in LPS-stimulated macrophages and IL-1β-damaged chondrocytes. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that DTF upregulated HIF1α and suppressed TNF and IL17 signaling pathways. In both MIA-induced acute and DMM-induced chronic OA models, DTF alleviated pain, reduced synovitis, and preserved cartilage integrity without systemic toxicity. This study presents a genetics-guided nanotherapeutic approach, highlighting a translational pathway from population-based evidence to targeted OA treatment.

articles.title: Targeting RSK2 reverses endocrine resistance in ER-positive breast cancer via inhibiting the c-Myc-ERBB4 signaling pathway.
articles.abstract: Endocrine therapy remains a major adjuvant treatment for estrogen receptor (ER)-positive breast cancer, yet its clinical efficacy is frequently compromised by primary or acquired resistance, leading to tumor recurrence and poor prognosis. In this study, we identified RSK2 (p90 ribosomal S6 kinase 2) as a critical mediator of endocrine resistance in ER-positive breast cancer. Analysis of publicly available datasets and our clinical samples revealed that high expression of RSK2 is associated with unfavorable outcomes in patients treated with endocrine therapy. RSK2 overexpression confers resistance to both tamoxifen and fulvestrant, two commonly used ER antagonists. We show that RSK2 is upregulated in tamoxifen-resistant breast cancer cells compared to parental controls, and that RSK2 knockdown restores tamoxifen sensitivity and inhibits tumor progression in vitro and in vivo. Further, we found that RSK2 stabilizes c-Myc by phosphorylating it at serine 62, thereby enhancing the transcriptional of ERBB4, which in turn promotes ER-driven proliferation. Moreover, ‌positive correlations between RSK2, c-Myc and ERBB4‌ were observed in ER-positive breast cancer specimens from patients. Notably, by screening the FDA-approved drug library, we identified emetine, an anti-protozoan drug used in the treatment of ameobiasis, as a potential RSK2 degrader and a modulator of tamoxifen resistance in preclinical models. Together, these findings establish the RSK2-c-Myc-ERBB4 axis as a therapeutic vulnerability in endocrine resistant breast cancer, and propose the repurposing of emetine as a sensitizer of endocrine therapy for breast cancer.

articles.title: A novel peptide-drug conjugate GV-K for anti-colorectal cancer therapy via mitochondrial apoptosis.
articles.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) has the second-highest mortality rate, seriously threatening human health. Despite many advances in the field of CRC therapy, an effective cure is yet to be found. As a more potent alternative to the conventional small-molecule anti-cancer drugs, peptide-drug conjugates (PDCs) have emerged as a new class of anticancer agents. Based on the principle of drug target co-screening, our study identified a novel CRC affinity peptide, GV12, which specifically bound to the protein ANXA2 on CRC cells using phage display technology. Moreover, the peptide GV12 was capable of penetrating CRC cells but without exerting cytotoxic effects. We constructed a peptide-drug conjugate, designated GV-K, composed of GV12 and the pro-apoptotic peptide D-(KLA)2, which demonstrated significant anti-CRC effects both in vitro and in vivo. GV-K targeted the membrane protein ANXA2 and primarily internalized into CRC cells via receptor-mediated endocytosis. Subsequently, GV-K was successfully localized to the mitochondria and thereby induced apoptosis of CRC cells by triggering the cytochrome C-Apaf-1-Caspase signaling pathway. These findings reveal a novel PDC, GV-K, which targets the membrane protein ANXA2 to internalize and induce apoptosis in CRC cells, suggesting a promising strategy for targeted therapy of CRC.

articles.title: Development of 68Ga-labeled macrocyclic peptide for targeting stimulator of interferon genes.
articles.abstract: The stimulator of interferon genes (STING) plays a vital role in innate immunity and is a promising anticancer target. Visualizing STING expression is essential for optimizing and guiding STING-targeted immunotherapies. This study aimed to design and develop macrocyclic peptide radiotracers for evaluating STING expression within the tumor microenvironment. A series of macrocyclic peptide-targeted STING radiotracers ([68Ga]Ga-FMAD, [68Ga]Ga-FMTD, [68Ga]Ga-FMT2D, and [68Ga]Ga-FMT3D) were synthesized by modifying the amino acid sequences and linkers. The radiotracers exhibited high radiochemical yield, radiochemical purity, and molar activity. PET imaging of [68Ga]Ga-FMAD and [68Ga]Ga-FMTD showed suboptimal tumor uptake, indicating limited STING-targeting efficacy. [68Ga]Ga-FMT3D demonstrated tumor uptake comparable to that of [68Ga]Ga-FMT2D while exhibiting superior pharmacokinetic properties, as indicated by a higher tumor-to-muscle (T/M) ratio. The tumor uptake values of [68Ga]Ga-FMT2D and [68Ga]Ga-FMT3D significantly decreased after NNK-2 (STING-specific binding compound) preadministration, indicating STING-specific targeting. The competition assays demonstrated high affinities, with IC50 values of 8.81 and 5.25 nmol/L for [68Ga]Ga-FMT2D and [68Ga]Ga-FMT3D, respectively. Furthermore, tumor uptake of [68Ga]Ga-FMT3D was significantly correlated with STING protein levels in the doxorubicin-treated model. Consequently, [68Ga]Ga-FMT3D, exhibiting high affinity for and specificity to STING, possesses favorable pharmacokinetics, serving as a promising tool for quantifying STING expression within the tumor microenvironment.

articles.title: SARS-CoV-2 inhibits EBV-dependent tumor proliferation through PLpro-mediated degradation of EBNA1.
articles.abstract: Co-circulation of multiple viruses within a host can produce pathological outcomes distinct from those of single-virus infections. Over 700 million documented severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infections during the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic indicate frequent co-circulation of SARS-CoV-2 with other human viruses. However, how SARS-CoV-2 infection influences other viral infections remains unclear. In this study, we investigated how the proteolytic activity of SARS-CoV-2 papain-like protease (PLpro) influences infection by other human viruses. In silico analysis identified candidate PLpro cleavage sites across numerous viral proteins, and biochemical assays confirmed that PLpro catalyzes the degradation of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) nuclear antigen 1 (EBNA1) in a manner requiring its protease activity. Both ectopic PLpro expression and SARS-CoV-2 infection reduced EBNA1 abundance, leading to reactivation of latent EBV. Given the essential role of EBNA1 in maintaining EBV-associated tumorigenesis, SARS-CoV-2 and PLpro-mediated degradation of EBNA1 can be translated into an inhibitory effect on EBV-driven tumor proliferation. These findings establish a molecular mechanism by which SARS-CoV-2 PLpro disrupts EBV latency and suppresses EBV-associated tumorigenesis, positioning EBNA1 as a potential therapeutic target in EBV-related malignancies.

articles.title: Orally delivered exosome-like nanoparticles from Tetrastigma hemsleyanum Diels et Gilg remodel the gut-tumor immune axis to activate antitumor immunity.
articles.abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is constrained by an immunologically "cold" tumor microenvironment (TME), limiting the benefits of immune checkpoint blockade. Here we develop a safe, orally delivered nanotherapeutic platform based on exosome-like nanoparticles derived from Tetrastigma hemsleyanum Diels et Gilg (TNPs). Owing to their biogenic vesicular architecture, TNPs exhibit excellent gastrointestinal stability, biocompatibility, and preferential uptake by intestinal antigen-presenting cells, thereby overcoming key barriers of oral delivery. Oral TNPs induce Th1-skewed immune activation and remodel gut microbiota, which collectively drive systemic immune reprogramming. In TNBC, these gut-initiated responses increase CD8+ and IFN-γ + T-cell infiltration, favor M1-like macrophage polarization, and reduce regulatory T cells, converting "cold" tumors into an immune-inflamed phenotype. Mechanistically, TNPs attenuate IFN-γ-induced PD-L1 upregulation via STAT1 suppression, mitigating adaptive immune resistance. Consequently, TNPs synergize with anti-PD-L1 therapy to enhance tumor regression without additional toxicity. This work establishes a natural exosome-inspired oral nanoplatform that couples drug-delivery advantages with potent immunomodulation through the gut-tumor immune axis, highlighting its translational potential for sensitizing refractory cancers to immune checkpoint blockade.

articles.title: Biomimetic tumor microenvironment-responsive prodrug amplifies photoimmunotherapy via TLR2 agonist.
articles.abstract: Toll-like receptors (TLRs), pivotal mediators bridging innate and adaptive immunity, form potent combinatorial platforms with photodynamic therapy (PDT) to achieve synergistic immunotherapy against malignancies. Herein, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved photosensitizer methylene blue (MB) was conjugated with a novel small-molecule TLR2 agonist via a glutathione-responsive disulfide bond, constructing a tumor microenvironment (TME)-redox-responsive prodrug (MB-SS-Z1-NH2). Co-assembly with amphiphilic PEG-PLGA yielded MZ-NPs, which acquired tumor-homing specificity through B16-F10 membrane camouflage (CCM@MZ-NPs). This biomimetic prodrug exhibits excellent biocompatibility and tumor targeting ability, allowing for selective activation within the TME and specific elimination of tumor cells through PDT. Crucially, TLR2 agonists delivered by CCM@MZ-NPs cooperated with tumor antigens to significantly enhance antigen presentation, thereby reversing TME immunosuppression and promoting the transition from immunologically "cold" to "hot" tumors. In vivo studies demonstrated that CCM@MZ-NPs leveraged TLR2 agonist to concurrently activate systemic immune responses and amplify PDT-mediated direct tumor destruction, effectively suppressing melanoma growth. Furthermore, primary tumor treatment induced a systemic antitumor immune response associated with long-term protective immunity, establishing sustained protection against distant tumor progression. This study pioneers the integration of TLR2 agonists with PDT nanotechnology, proposing a transformative combinatorial immunotherapy strategy through synchronous tumor eradication and immune microenvironment reprogramming.

articles.title: Dual-mode hepatoprotective nanoplatform combines ROS scavenging and FGF21 activation for precision acute liver injury therapy.
articles.abstract: To address the intertwined pathologies of oxidative stress, immune dysregulation, and lipid metabolic disorders in acute liver injury (ALI), we engineered an innovative nanosystem: M2@SAM-F21. M2@SAM-F21 features an M2 macrophage membrane coating encapsulating diselenide-bridged mesoporous silica nanoparticles for silymarin and FGF21 plasmid DNA codelivery, enabling synergistic multidimensional treatment. First, reactive oxygen species (ROS)-responsive oxidative stress is mitigated. Diselenide bonds undergo ROS-triggered cleavage, achieving precise silymarin release that efficiently scavenges multiple ROS types, significantly mitigating hepatic oxidative damage. Simultaneously, FGF21 drives immune reprogramming. Efficiently expressed FGF21 protein drives macrophage polarization toward the M2 anti-inflammatory phenotype, effectively reducing proinflammatory cytokine levels, with TNF-α decreased to 61 pg/mL and IL-6 reduced to 20 pg/mL, while increasing IL-10 to 68 pg/mL to reverse the immune microenvironment imbalance. In addition, metabolic homeostasis is restored. Activated fatty acid oxidation pathways substantially decrease serum concentrations of total cholesterol (TC) to 4.984 mmol/L and triglycerides (TG) to 0.586 mmol/L, and almost reduce hepatocellular lipid droplet accumulation by 76%, resolving metabolic dysregulation. In both alcoholic and drug-induced ALI models, M2@SAM-F21 demonstrates exceptional hepatoprotection. For example, it significantly restores serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) to 46.6 U/L and aminotransferase (AST) to 180 U/L in the alcoholic ALI model, while markedly alleviating histopathological vacuolization and steatosis, with biological distribution imaging confirming inflammation-targeted accumulation and proteomic analysis further elucidating therapeutic mechanisms. Exhibiting superior biosafety and dual therapeutic-prophylactic potential, this system serves as a pioneering paradigm that integrates targeted delivery, intelligent release, and multipathway synergy for ALI treatment.

articles.title: MS-DDF: An intelligent mass spectrometry framework tailored for overcoming the in vivo analytical bottleneck in animal-derived medicines.
articles.abstract: In vivo analysis of animal-derived medicines remains challenging due to poor chromatographic behavior and low mass spectrometry response. Chemical derivatization is commonly used to enhance the detection but produces complex datasets requiring advanced processing. Herein, we developed Mass Spectrometry Deep-refine Derivatization Filter (MS-DDF), an instrument-agnostic, intelligent post-processing workflow providing an advanced approach for in vivo analysis of animal-derived medicines. MS-DDF includes three functional modules: system noise subtraction to eliminate instrumental background, endogenous interference subtraction to remove interferences from endogenous components, and combinatorial peak matching enables efficient extraction of derivatized target components. As a proof of concept, we adopted MS-DDF to investigate Eupolyphaga sinensis Walker, to validate its suitability for in vivo analysis of components in animal-derived medicines, with simple operation and broad applicability. Additionally, MS-DDF can serve as an analytical platform for metabolomics studies across different functional groups.

articles.title: Targeting cancer-associated neutrophils with biomimetic nano-vaccines loaded with mRNA can enhance the efficacy of immunotherapy for hepatocellular carcinoma.
articles.abstract: Neutrophils exhibit significant plasticity within the tumor microenvironment (TME), such as promoting immune suppression, tumor growth, and metastasis. Although various nano drug delivery systems targeting neutrophils have been developed based on their tumor chemotaxis, few studies have focused on designing nano-vaccines that specifically target and activate neutrophils to exert anti-tumor effects, mainly due to the lack of specific targets. To address these issues, we genetically engineered tumor cell membranes to first overexpress the CD300LD protein, which was subsequently coated onto the surface of liposomes. Additionally, we encoded and delivered the cytokine IL-36γ, which can effectively activate neutrophils, thus constructing an mRNA-based biomimetic nanovaccine, termed CMNPs (cell-membrane coated mRNA nanovaccine platform), which is designed to elicit potent anti-tumor immunity by targeted activation of neutrophils. Through analysis of single-cell public databases, we discovered that neutrophils in the TME express CD300LD receptors at significantly higher levels compared to other immune cells. Consequently, we further transduced tumor cells with lentivirus to induce overexpression of the CD300LD protein and utilized cell membrane biomimetic technology to modify the surface of CMNPs. The modified CMNPs can specifically target neutrophils via the extracellular domain (ECD) of the CD300LD protein. Upon targeted delivery of CMNPs to neutrophils in the TME, the internally encoded mRNA, fused with albumin and IL-36γ, is transcribed and translated. Since albumin prolongs the half-life of the cytokine, IL-36γ continuously activates neutrophils via the IL-36R receptor on their surface, enhancing their tumoricidal functions and activating other immune cells. Experimental results confirmed that CMNPs effectively activate neutrophils, leading to robust anti-tumor immune responses and tumor growth inhibition. Compared to the control group, CMNPs increased mouse survival rates to 85%. Collectively, the CMNPs vaccine demonstrates broad therapeutic efficacy and remarkable functional diversity, not only improving the effectiveness of immunotherapy but also providing a novel strategy for neutrophil-targeted tumor immunotherapy.

articles.title: Concurrent loss of RB1 facilitates EGFR-TKI resistance in EGFR-mutant lung cancer by modulating histone crotonylation.
articles.abstract: Lung cancer harboring epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations exhibits marked heterogeneity in clinical responses to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs), indicating that co-occurring genetic alterations critically influence therapeutic outcomes. However, the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, we modeled frequent EGFR co-alterations using CRISPR-mediated gene knockout and Tet-On-based gene overexpression in two EGFR-mutant cell lines. Functional screening across cell lines and patient-derived organoids revealed that concurrent loss of retinoblastoma 1 (RB1) significantly reduced sensitivity to EGFR-TKIs. Integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses further demonstrated that RB1 deficiency induced extensive metabolic reprogramming, leading to decreased intracellular crotonyl-CoA levels and reduced histone crotonylation. Among multiple crotonylation sites, histone H3 lysine 23 crotonylation (H3K23cr) emerged as a critical determinant of EGFR-TKI responsiveness. Mechanistically, decreased H3K23cr was associated with transcriptional repression of PEBP1 and reduced expression of the PEBP1-encoded Raf kinase inhibitor protein (RKIP), thereby sustaining RAF/MEK/ERK pathway activation and attenuating EGFR-TKI efficacy. Importantly, pharmacological restoration of histone crotonylation or inhibition of MAPK signaling effectively resensitized EGFR/RB1 co-mutant models to EGFR-TKIs. Taken together, our findings identify a metabolic-epigenetic mechanism linking RB1 loss to reduced histone crotonylation and EGFR-TKI resistance, highlighting therapeutically actionable vulnerabilities in EGFR/RB1 co-mutant lung cancer.

articles.title: A peptide-based nano-PROTAC synergistically driving ferroptosis-immunotherapy in triple-negative breast cancer.
articles.abstract: Ferroptosis, an emerging mechanism of cell death, provides new targets for the treatment of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). Glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), a key regulator of ferroptosis, is a promising therapeutic target for TNBC. Given that GPX4 is often considered "undruggable", proteolysis targeting chimeras (PROTACs) offer a powerful means for its degradation. However, conventional PROTACs often face challenges in achieving precise localization and potent activation in vivo. Herein, we engineered a peptide-based nano-PROTAC, named CMVG, which couples VHL- and GPX4-binding peptides with iron-based metal-organic frameworks via a "click" reaction and loads the photosensitizer chlorin e6 (Ce6). CMVG enhances ferroptosis through a dual mechanism: it degrades GPX4 via its PROTAC function to initiate ferroptosis, while generating reactive oxygen species under laser irradiation to mediate photodynamic therapy, thereby intensifying oxidative stress and accelerating ferroptosis. Furthermore, the ferroptosis induced by CMVG is highly immunogenic, triggering immunogenic cell death and reshaping the tumor immune microenvironment, ultimately boosting the anti-TNBC immune response. Additionally, CMVG exhibits excellent targeting and biocompatibility, enabling MRI-guided tumor treatment. This work presents the first peptide-based nano-PROTAC for GPX4 degradation, overcoming major limitations of conventional PROTACs, and offers a promising integrated strategy for treating TNBC.

articles.title: A probiotic-drug cascade system for inflammatory bowel disease via tryptophan metabolism and gut microbiome remodeling.
articles.abstract: The development of oral therapeutics capable of improving tryptophan metabolism and restoring gut microbiome homeostasis is vital for effective inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) management. Despite the significant advancements in bacteriotherapy for IBD, current strategies often suffer from limited functionalities and compromised efficacy due to the multifaceted nature of gastrointestinal tract physiology and pathology. Here, we propose an acid-resistant and microenvironment-responsive probiotic-drug codelivery system (BS@MPN-BBR@S100) based on the metal-phenolic network (MPN). Following oral administration, the dual MPN-S100 coating significantly enhances probiotic survival in the face of gastrointestinal challenges, including gastric acid and proteases, promoting targeted adhesion to colonic lesions. Impressively, the loaded berberine (BBR) is released in a targeted, calprotectin (CP)-responsive manner at disease sites, thereby effectively restoring intestinal barrier function by remodeling tryptophan metabolism. In a murine model of colitis, BS@MPN-BBR@S100 effectively alleviated disease symptoms by regulating tryptophan metabolism, reshaping microbiome homeostasis, and alleviating oxidative stress. Overall, this study addresses key bottlenecks in oral probiotics and drug delivery, offering a promising strategy for developing effective therapeutics against IBD.

articles.title: Activation of KIF18B-MYC axis by autophagic CUL3 degradation promotes copper imbalance essential for gastric cancer progression.
articles.abstract: Imbalance of copper homeostasis leads to cancer progression, while its molecular basis and treatment approaches in gastric cancer remain elusive. Herein, MYC proto-oncogene and kinesin family member 18 B (KIF18B) were identified as transcriptional suppressors of metallothionein (MT) genes, thereby driving copper-mediated aggressiveness and ferroptosis resistance in gastric cancer. Mechanistically, KIF18B was stabilized via p62-mediated autophagic degradation of E3 ubiquitin ligase cullin 3 (CUL3), which activated MYC via physical interaction to repress expression of copper storage genes MT2A and MT1X, resulting in elevation of free copper, subsequent up-regulation of pyruvate carboxylase (PC) and ferritin heavy chain 1 (FTH1), increase of tricarboxylic acid cycle for energy production, and decrease of ferroptosis in gastric cancer. KIF18B facilitated growth or aggressiveness and inhibited ferroptosis of gastric cancer cells via increasing MYC activity. An inhibitory peptide was established to block interplay between KIF18B and MYC, which suppressed growth, invasion, or metastasis and induced ferroptosis of gastric cancer. High KIF18B, MYC, PC, or FTH1 expression was associated with poor prognosis, while low CUL3, MT2A, or MT1X levels were linked to unfavorable outcome of gastric cancer patients. These findings suggest that activation of KIF18B‒MYC axis by autophagic CUL3 degradation promotes copper imbalance essential for gastric cancer progression.

articles.title: Intestinal epithelial CSE-derived H2S alleviates food allergy via modulating the IL-25/ILC2 axis.
articles.abstract: Hydrogen sulfide (H2S), an endogenous gasotransmitter, has garnered increasing attention for its role in modulating immune responses and intestinal barrier function. In this study, diminished jejunal H2S levels and expression of its synthesizing enzyme cystathionine gamma-lyase (CSE) in intestinal epithelium were observed in ovalbumin (OVA)-induced food allergic mice. CSE deficiency aggravated OVA-induced food allergy by activating the IL-25/ILC2 axis and enhancing type 2 immune responses, effects that were reversed by exogenous H2S supplementation. Furthermore, H2S treatment suppressed intestinal epithelial cell-derived IL-25 expression by inhibiting c-Jun. IL-25 neutralization attenuated ILC2-driven type 2 immune responses and alleviated allergic symptoms in OVA-challenged CSE-knockout (Cse -/- ) mice. Moreover, ILC2 inhibition diminished type 2 cytokine production and disrupted the IL-25 feedback loop, thereby ameliorating food allergy in Cse -/- mice. These findings highlight that intestinal epithelial CSE-derived H2S alleviates food allergy via the IL-25/ILC2 axis and serves as a potential therapeutic target for allergic diseases.

articles.title: Pathological progression features-guided biphasic drug delivery supramolecular hydrogel for synergistic cartilage protection in osteoarthritis.
articles.abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) remains a major clinical challenge due to its complex pathogenesis and the current lack of effective therapies capable of halting the progressive degradation of cartilage. Our bioinformatics analysis reveals that synovial inflammation precedes cartilage degeneration in early-stage OA, and chondrocyte pyroptosis present in both early and late stages, further promoting cartilage degeneration. Based on these findings, we developed a novel pathological progression-guided biphasic drug delivery supramolecular hydrogel (SP Gel/DS@cLip) featured by dual cross-linking where both spermidine (SP) and disulfiram (DS)-loaded cationic liposomes (DS@cLip) actively participate in hydrogel network formation.
